rounds.proof_sketch: The mutation changes `float accum[4][4]` to `float accum[5][4]`. All loops accessing accum use hardcoded bounds: `for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++)` and `for (int j = 0; j < 4; j++)`. This means accum[4][*] (the extra row) is never written to during computation and never read from during output. The array bounds [0..3][0..3] are compile-time constants independent of input values.
rounds.survival_reason: The mutation allocates an extra row in the accumulator array (row index 4) that is completely unused by the kernel. All computation loops iterate with `i < 4` and `j < 4`, accessing only indices [0..3][0..3]. The initialization `{{0.0f}}` zeroes all elements including the unused row, but this has no effect on output. Since array access patterns are determined by hardcoded loop bounds rather than input-dependent values, no input tensor values can cause the kernel to access the extra row. The mutation is semantically equivalent because it changes memory layout without affecting any computation paths.
rounds.kill_strategy: This mutant is unkillable because it is semantically equivalent. The mutation only affects memory allocation (5 rows vs 4 rows in the accumulator), but all access patterns use fixed loop bounds of 4. No input values can trigger access to accum[4][*] since all loop conditions are compile-time constants `i < 4` and `j < 4`. The extra memory is allocated but never touched during execution.
rounds.recommendations: Mutation testing frameworks should implement dead-storage detection for array declarations where the mutated dimension exceeds all access indices. When array bounds are enlarged but all access patterns remain bounded by smaller compile-time constants, the mutation should be automatically classified as equivalent. This pattern (unused array expansion) is a common source of false-positive surviving mutants.
